claims.text: Q235 steel forms an initially protective iron-oxide scale at lower temperatures.
Above approximately 700 °C in salt-laden environments, the oxide scale on Q235 steel degrades because of thermal-expansion mismatch and salt-induced spallation.
Degradation and spallation of the oxide scale accelerate corrosion of Q235 steel.
At lower temperatures or under less aggressive conditions, the oxide layer remains relatively intact and moderates further degradation.
The proposed specimens are as-received rolled Q235 coupons with mill scale removed and stored in ambient laboratory air before testing.
A controlled study can expose salt-coated and salt-free Q235 specimens to the same stepped temperature profile from room temperature to approximately 900 °C.
SEM/EDS and XRD can be used to characterize oxide-scale structure and composition during the study.
Below approximately 600 °C, Q235 develops a relatively coherent oxide film.
A coherent low-temperature oxide film limits iron-ion diffusion and corrosion.
Above approximately 700 °C in salt-laden environments, the Q235 oxide layer spalls.
Molten salt partially dissolves or fluxes the oxide layer at high temperature.
Loss of oxide integrity permits corrosive agents to penetrate and causes accelerated material loss.
Salt-laden Q235 will exhibit minimal corrosion up to approximately 600 °C and a sharp increase in mass loss and localized degradation at or above 700 °C.
Salt-free or lower-temperature Q235 controls will show smaller mass change and less oxide-layer disruption.
Low-alloy or stainless steels tested under identical conditions will show less oxide spallation and lower high-temperature mass loss than Q235 steel.
The proposed effect is strongest when molten or near-molten salt contacts Q235 at temperatures of at least 700 °C.
Q235 is susceptible because it lacks sufficient alloying elements that form stable protective oxide scales.
The oxide-breakdown transition temperature depends on Q235 compositional variation and salt chemistry.
